title: Trap-Quenched Matter-Wave Optics for Dual Species Lensing
authors: Gabriel Müller, Timothé Estrampes, Claudia Puertas González, Jannik Ströhle, David B. Reinhardt, Dana Codruta Marinica, Ethan R. Elliott, Jason R. Williams, Nathan Lundblad, Eric Charron, Ernst M. Rasel, Matthias Meister, Wolfgang P. Schleich, Naceur Gaaloul, Nicholas P. Bigelow
abstract: Dual-species atom interferometry in space promises precise tests of the Universality of Free Fall (UFF), with a sensitivity that grows quadratically with the extended interrogation time accessible in weightlessness. These tests demand exquisite control over the expansion energies of both condensed sources as well as over their differential center-of-mass dynamics. We propose a trap-quenched collimation technique featuring in-trap excitations of collective modes compatible with state-of-the-art atom-chip setups. Using NASA's Cold Atom Laboratory aboard the International Space Station, we demonstrate it on a single-species $^{87}$Rb condensate. By controlling the center-of-mass release dynamics we observe free expansion times up to 700 ms and measure a two-dimensional expansion energy of $k_B \cdot 78\pm 9 \;\mathrm{pK}$ in the imaging plane. A detailed model of the magnetically-induced dynamics indicates that this corresponds to a two-dimensional expansion energy of about $k_B \cdot 15^{+12}_{-5}\; \mathrm{pK}$ along two of the condensate's eigenaxes. Finally, we theoretically study this trap-quenched collimation scheme for a $^{41}$K-$^{87}$Rb mixture, predicting a simultaneous collimation that meets the expansion energy requirements for a state-of-the-art UFF test at the $10^{-15}$ accuracy level.
summary: The paper details the development and application of trap-quenched collimation for Bose-Einstein condensates to enhance atom interferometry tests of the Universality of Free Fall. By combining novel experimental techniques with sophisticated modeling, the authors predict that dual-species BECs can achieve the necessary low expansion energies required for unprecedented precision in space-based fundamental physics measurements.
main_problem: The primary goal is to improve tests of the Universality of Free Fall (UFF) using Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs), which requires exquisite control over expansion energies and center-of-mass dynamics for dual-species systems.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a trap-quenched collimation technique on single-species BECs in space, theoretically predicting simultaneous collimation for a ${}^{41}	ext{K}–{}^{87}	ext{Rb}$ mixture that meets the energy requirements for $10^{-15}$ accuracy UFF tests.
method: The research combines experimental implementation of trap-quenched collimation with detailed theoretical modeling, using effective models and *ab initio* simulations to track BEC size dynamics during trapping and free expansion.
model_or_system: The physical system is a BEC trapped in an atom chip setup, tested aboard the International Space Station. The model involves simulating time-dependent magnetic field interactions via gauged atom chip potentials and using effective models for post-release ballistic/semi-free expansion.
key_observables: 2D and 3D expansion energies ($E_{exp}$), Center-of-Mass (CoM) oscillation dynamics, and the Thomas-Fermi radii of the BEC during Time-of-Flight (ToF).
important_parameters: Expansion energy levels ($\sim k_B \cdot 78 	ext{ pK}$ for single species; $\sim 43-48 	ext{ pK}$ for dual species), interrogation time up to $700 	ext{ ms}$, and target accuracy of $10^{-15}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting complex dynamics using effective models, which requires approximations like assuming no inter-species interaction initially and simplifying the magnetic field gradients during ToF.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the trap-quenched collimation scheme (Fig. 1), CoM oscillation control (Fig. 2a/b), and comparisons between simulated vs. measured expansion energies in various reference frames (Fig. 3, Fig. 4).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from introducing the UFF test requirement to detailing the trap-quenched collimation technique, presenting single-species measurements, developing sophisticated models for size dynamics, and finally extending the theory to predict optimal dual-species performance.
why_interesting: This work represents a cutting edge intersection of quantum sensing and advanced atomic physics, demonstrating how precise control over matter-wave expansion in space can push fundamental measurement limits beyond terrestrial capabilities.
